analysis.one_liner: Lets local regulators block basic cable rate hikes above 5% or inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after four subcommittee hearings, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Cable operators had been deregulated by a 1984 law, and the bill's findings noted that basic cable rates had risen at least twice as fast as inflation since then [S3]. This bill would have let state or local franchising authorities require cable companies to get approval before putting through any basic-cable rate increase larger than 5% or the rise in the Consumer Price Index, whichever was higher, counting combined increases within a year as one [S2] [S3]. It was never voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, especially households on fixed incomes who the bill's findings say bore 'an unreasonable hardship' from rate increases, would have gained a local check on price hikes for basic cable service [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Basic cable subscribers, especially fixed-income households

how_it_helps.text: State or local franchising authorities could require a cable operator to get prior approval before any basic-cable rate increase exceeding the higher of 5% or the trailing 12-month CPI increase [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that since the 1984 Cable Act deregulated the industry, basic cable rates had risen by at least twice the rate of the Consumer Price Index while the CPI itself rose 18.4%, leaving consumers 'no recourse' against an 'unregulated monopoly' [S3].
Two or more rate increases within any 12-month period would count as a single increase, so operators could not evade the threshold by spreading out small hikes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, who had operated without federal rate regulation since 1984 and would have needed local sign-off for large basic-rate increases; some of the compliance cost could have been passed to subscribers or reflected in slower expansion of service.

drawbacks.text: Re-imposing local rate approval on a recently deregulated industry could have discouraged operators from building out systems or adding channels, one of the stated rationales for the 1984 deregulation the bill cites [S3].
The bill covers only basic cable service, so costs could have shifted to premium tiers and other charges outside the approval threshold.

The provision is permissive rather than mandatory: it authorizes state and local authorities to require approval but does not itself cap rates, leaving protection uneven depending on where a subscriber lived [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing basic cable rates rising at roughly double inflation under what the bill's own findings call an unregulated monopoly, a local check on increases above inflation was a real, targeted benefit, and the modest burden fell on a single industry [S3]. The design was narrow — only basic service, and only if local authorities chose to act — so its protections would have been uneven, but the core trade-off of slightly constrained operators versus a price check for millions of subscribers favored consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, moved to its telecommunications subcommittee, got four hearings, and then died there without ever reaching a committee or floor vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lewis Payne of Virginia introduced the bill on April 26, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
Eight days later it went to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, which held hearings on March 1, April 19, May 9, and May 16, 1990 [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed; the bill was never reported out and expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators came out ahead: they kept the unregulated-monopoly pricing the bill described, free to raise basic rates without local approval, while subscribers continued to pay increases that had been outpacing inflation [S3] [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable operators, who kept unregulated pricing

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape is hard to read: the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill simply ran out of runway in committee rather than losing a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have ended cable operators' free hand on basic-rate increases, requiring local approval for any hike above 5% or inflation. Their interest in blocking it ran directly against subscribers paying increases the bill says ran twice the inflation rate.
Local regulators would have gained power to negotiate or reject large basic-rate increases on behalf of their residents. That power serves the same subscribers who would benefit from it.
